item.title: Qereqeretabua announced as NFP Deputy Leader
item.description: Lenora Qereqeretabua has been announced as National Federation Party Deputy Leader. Qereqeretabua was announced as Deputy Leader by NFP Leader, Professor Biman Prasad.
item.content:encoded:
Lenora Qereqeretabua has been announced as National Federation Party Deputy Leader.

Qereqeretabua was announced as Deputy Leader by NFP Leader, Professor Biman Prasad.

Speaking after the announcement, Qereqeretabua says her focus is on three main issues - fixing health, fixing education and fixing the economy.

She confirms she will remain in politics and will remain with the NFP.

Qereqeretabua says voters must think carefully and people need to remember that NFP only has 5 votes in a 40 member government.

She says they are aiming to be the party with majority of the votes in the next general elections.

item.title: Five arrested after suspected drugs found at Narain Jetty
item.description: Five people have been arrested after substances believed to be marijuana were discovered during a raid at Narain Jetty in Suva early this morning. The operation involved the Totogo Operations team, the Dog Unit and the Fiji Detector Dog Unit, who searched an inter-island vessel.
item.content:encoded:
Five people have been arrested after substances believed to be marijuana were discovered during a raid at Narain Jetty in Suva early this morning.

The operation involved the Totogo Operations team, the Dog Unit and the Fiji Detector Dog Unit, who searched an inter-island vessel.

Police say plastic bags containing dried leaves believed to be marijuana were found hidden inside a vehicle.

They say a further search by K9 officers led to the arrest of five suspects who were allegedly found in possession of substances believed to be marijuana.

All five were escorted to the Totogo Police Station, while the seized substances have been sent for analysis.

Members of the public can report crime or share information by calling 1681.

item.title: Health Ministry strengthens water supply plans for health facilities amid dry weather
item.description: As dry weather conditions continue to affect parts of the country, the Ministry of Health is strengthening plans to ensure a continuous water supply to health facilities across Fiji, particularly in rural areas. Minister for Health and Medical Services, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu says the Ministry places great importance on having plans in place to maintain water supplies at health facilities in bo
item.content:encoded:
As dry weather conditions continue to affect parts of the country, the Ministry of Health is strengthening plans to ensure a continuous water supply to health facilities across Fiji, particularly in rural areas.

Minister for Health and Medical Services, Dr Ratu Atonio Lalabalavu says the Ministry places great importance on having plans in place to maintain water supplies at health facilities in both major towns and rural areas.

Responding to questions from fijivillage News, Lalabalavu says this is part of the Ministry's Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) programme.

He says many health facilities already have backup water storage systems in place to ensure services can continue when the regular water supply is disrupted.

item.title: More research needed before Fiji decides on deep-sea mining
item.description: More research is needed before any decision is made on deep-sea mining in Fiji’s waters, with the Government stressing the importance of protecting the ocean and the interests of its people. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce and Business Development Manoa Kamikamica says Fiji must first understand the resources beneath its ocean, the risks involved and how any future deci
item.content:encoded:
More research is needed before any decision is made on deep-sea mining in Fiji’s waters, with the Government stressing the importance of protecting the ocean and the interests of its people.

Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Industries, Commerce and Business Development Manoa Kamikamica says Fiji must first understand the resources beneath its ocean, the risks involved and how any future decisions could affect communities and the environment.

Speaking at the opening of the Science, Technology and Resources (STAR) Conference 2026 in Suva today, Kamikamica says having a legal framework for deep-sea mining does not mean Fiji has decided to go ahead with it.

He says any decision must be based on scientific evidence, transparency and what is best for the people and the ocean.

Kamikamica says global demand for minerals such as cobalt, nickel and rare earth elements is increasing because of new technology and the move towards cleaner energy.

He says Pacific countries must have a strong voice in discussions about their ocean resources rather than allowing others to make decisions on their behalf.

The Deputy Prime Minister also highlighted the importance of the ocean to everyday life, particularly through trade, businesses and employment.

He says ports play an important role in bringing goods into the country and helping local producers connect with overseas markets.

Kamikamica says having reliable information, proper infrastructure and clear rules will help attract investment while also protecting communities and the environment.

He says the benefits of developing natural resources should reach the people, and communities should not be left to carry the costs.

The Deputy Prime Minister also called for greater investment in young Pacific scientists, saying their knowledge and skills will be important in making decisions about the region’s resources in the years ahead.

He encouraged young scientists attending the conference to ask questions, share their knowledge and build connections that will help shape the future of the Pacific.

The STAR Conference brings together government officials, scientists, researchers, universities and development partners from Fiji, the Pacific and other parts of the world.

The conference will focus on energy, minerals, ocean resources and the importance of using science to support development.

Kamikamica says the gathering provides an opportunity for Pacific countries to share knowledge, strengthen partnerships and make informed decisions that will benefit their people and future generations.

item.title: We Unite Fiji says constitutional reform must benefit ordinary Fijians, not politicians
item.description: The proposed Constitution (Amendment) Bill must deliver stronger democracy, protect human rights, ensure accountability and safeguard the interests of ordinary Fijians, rather than benefit those holding political power. This was the message from the We Unite Fiji Party during their submission before the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, where the party raised co
item.content:encoded:
The proposed Constitution (Amendment) Bill must deliver stronger democracy, protect human rights, ensure accountability and safeguard the interests of ordinary Fijians, rather than benefit those holding political power.

This was the message from the We Unite Fiji Party during their submission before the Parliamentary Special Committee on the Constitution (Amendment) Bill, where the party raised concerns over several provisions and called for greater clarity, legal safeguards and public consultation before the Bill is adopted.

Party Leader Ruveni Nadalo says Fiji needs a constitutional reform that strengthens equal citizenship, protects customary land and culture, and makes every public institution accountable to the people.

Nadalo acknowledged that the Bill contains worthwhile objectives but says it is not ready for adoption in its present form.

He says Fiji had gone through four constitutions since independence in 1970 - in 1970, 1990, 1997 and 2013, and stresses the importance of ensuring the country does not continue experiencing constitutional changes without addressing the underlying issues.

Nadalo is urging Fijians, regardless of ethnicity, religion, political affiliation or social background, to consider five key questions when assessing the proposed reforms.

These include whether the new arrangements will give ordinary citizens a stronger voice in decisions affecting their future, ensure political leaders and public officials are accountable, support economic development, guarantee equal treatment and protect the interests of future generations.

He says constitutional reform should improve the everyday lives of ordinary Fijians, ensure the law applies fairly regardless of a person's position, wealth or political influence, and strengthen the independence and resources of public institutions.

Party General Secretary Satish Kumar raised concerns about the legality of the amendment process, particularly the change from the three-quarter majority requirement under the 2013 Constitution to a two-thirds majority following a Supreme Court decision.

Kumar says the party wants greater clarity on the legal basis of the amendment process, stressing that Parliament exercises legislative authority while the Supreme Court operates under the Constitution.

He says the party's concerns also extends to provisions relating to immunity, warning that some existing protections are not clearly preserved in the proposed Bill.

Kumar questioned the relationship between provisions retaining parts of the existing constitutional arrangements and those repealing the 2013 Promulgation Decree.

He says this raises questions about whether protected provisions are being repealed or reduced, and recommends that a reasoned legal assessment be published, alongside clear provisions outlining which protections will remain.

The party also raised concerns about the proposed immunity arrangements, particularly the possibility of immunity extending across future governments.

Kumar says the Bill should establish an explicit historical cut-off and make clear that the new Constitution would not create additional immunity for conduct beyond that date.

On future constitutional amendments, the party expressed concern that the proposed framework will allow Parliament to make changes through parliamentary supermajorities without a referendum.

Kumar says fundamental changes affecting citizens' rights, electoral equality, constitutional supremacy and judicial independence should require direct approval from the people.

The party further raised concerns about the relationship between the proposed Constitution's founding references to Christianity and family values and its provisions prohibiting the State from favouring any religious or non-religious belief.

They recommend that religious neutrality be expressly affirmed, with protections for the freedom to believe, change one's religion or hold no religious belief.

On the Bill of Rights, Kumar says the general test for limiting rights should apply consistently across all provisions, with any restrictions required to meet the principles of legality, necessity and proportionality .

He also called for clearer provisions allowing representatives, groups and public interest organisations to bring constitutional cases, alongside accessible court procedures, cost protection and practical access to legal aid.

The submission also questioned the proposed administrative justice provisions, including the exclusion of registered companies and the delayed commencement of certain protections.

Kumar says constitutional administrative justice protections should apply from the commencement of the Constitution and should be based on the exercise of public power or a public function, rather than the legal status of an organisation.

On detention, the party raised concerns about provisions allowing detention on grounds including vagrancy, addiction or suspected unsound mind, saying these should be subject to clear requirements of necessity, proportionality and regular judicial review.

They also recommend removing status-based detention linked to poverty or vagrancy and ensuring prompt access to the courts for people detained under any category.

The party is also calling for the removal of the provision allowing lawful and moderate chastisement of children, arguing that it could undermine protections against violence and harmful practices.

Kumar says the Constitution should protect children from all forms of corporal punishment and support positive discipline and appropriate child protection measures.

On freedom of expression, the party warns that restrictions relating to attacks on the dignity of respected offices or institutions, public morality and hate speech can potentially discourage criticism, journalism, academic debate and satire.

They recommend clearer definitions of prohibited incitement and stronger protection for public interest criticism and peaceful advocacy.

The submission also highlighted concerns over customary land and marine rights, particularly the need for a clear framework to resolve overlapping claims involving customary owners, State leases, existing permits, public infrastructure and customary access.
